s: 専門家の予想（　　）、今年の夏は例年より涼しかった。
en: Contrary to the experts' forecasts, this summer was cooler than usual.
why: 〜に反して: the outcome went the opposite way to a forecast or hope. Experts predicted heat; it was cool.
〜に沿って means following a plan or line. Weather does not follow a forecast on purpose.
〜に応じて means 'adjusting to' something that varies. A forecast is not something the summer adjusts to.
〜にこたえて means responding to a request or hope from people. The summer cannot answer one.
tell: 予想・期待・意図 plus an outcome that went the other way: に反して.

s: 社内の規則（　　）行為があった場合は、厳しく処分する。
en: Any act that breaks company rules will be dealt with strictly.
why: 〜に反する + noun: an act that goes against the rules. That is what gets punished.
〜に沿った means in line with the rules. Nobody is punished for following them.
〜に応じた means matched to something that varies. Rules are not a scale to match.
〜に基づく means grounded in the rules. Again, that would not be punished.
tell: Punishment ahead means the act broke the rule: 規則に反する.

s: 住民の強い願い（　　）、市は駅前の公園を駐車場にすることを決めた。
en: Against the residents' strong wishes, the city decided to turn the park by the station into a car park.
why: 〜に反して: the decision went against what residents wanted. Residents wish to keep a park, not lose it.
〜にこたえて means granting the wish. No resident strongly wishes to lose their park.
〜に応じて means adjusting in line with something that varies. The city did the opposite of the wish.
〜をもとに means using something as material or a basis. A wish is not material for a car park.
tell: A wish and an action that goes the other way: 願いに反して. Granting it would be にこたえて.

s: 当初の計画（　　）、新しい橋の完成は二年も遅れることになった。
en: Contrary to the original plan, the new bridge will be finished two whole years late.
why: 〜に反して: the plan said one date, reality went another way. 二年も遅れる is the clash.
〜に沿って means following the plan. A two-year delay does not follow it.
〜に先立って means before an event, as preparation. A plan is not an event to come before.
〜にわたって goes with a span of time or space (三年にわたって). A plan is not a span.
tell: Plan or forecast plus a result that broke it: 計画に反して.

s: インターネットは便利な（　　）、個人情報が漏れる危険もある。
en: The internet is convenient, but it also carries the risk of personal data leaking.
why: 〜反面: one thing with a good side (convenient) and a bad side (risk).
〜うえに stacks things of the same value, good with good or bad with bad. Here good meets bad.
〜ばかりか escalates in the same direction. Convenience does not escalate into danger.
〜以上 means 'since' and needs a duty or will after it. 危険もある is neither.
tell: Good side, then bad side of the same thing: 反面.

s: この薬はよく効く（　　）、眠くなるという副作用がある。
en: This medicine works well, but it has the side effect of making you drowsy.
why: 〜反面: the medicine's good side (it works) and its bad side (a side effect).
〜からには means 'now that' and needs a duty or resolve after it. A side effect is neither.
〜だけあって praises a result as expected. A side effect is not praise.
〜うちに means 'while it lasts, before it changes'. That makes no sense with a side effect.
tell: Works well, but a side effect: two sides of one thing, 反面.

s: この仕事は収入が安定している（　　）、休みが少ないのが不満だ。
en: This job pays a steady income, but I am unhappy that there are few days off.
why: 〜反面: the job's plus (steady pay) and its minus (few days off).
〜ばかりに blames one cause for a bad result. Steady pay does not cause few days off.
〜ことだし gives a reason for a decision or suggestion. 不満だ is neither.
〜たとたん needs a past verb and a sudden event. 安定している is a steady state.
tell: Plus, then minus, of the same job: 反面.

s: 都会の生活は刺激が多い（　　）、ストレスもたまりやすいと言えるだろう。
en: City life is stimulating, but you could say it is also easy to build up stress.
why: 〜反面: city life's good side (stimulation) and its bad side (stress).
〜からといって needs a denial after it (〜わけではない). The sentence ends in 言えるだろう.
〜末に needs a long process and its final result, with a verb in た形. 多い is not a process.
〜どころか says the opposite of X is true. The city still has lots of stimulation.
tell: One thing with a bright side and a dark side: 反面.

s: 子どもの数が減り続ける（　　）、高齢者の数は年々増えている。
en: While the number of children keeps falling, the number of older people grows every year.
why: 〜一方で sets two different things side by side: children going down, older people going up.
〜反面 shows two sides of ONE thing. Here there are two different groups.
〜うえに stacks two points in the same direction. These two trends go opposite ways.
〜最中に means 'right in the middle of' an action. A long trend is not one.
tell: Two different subjects, contrasted: 一方で. One subject, two sides: 反面.

s: 姉は社交的で友達が多い。（　　）、妹は一人で本を読むのが好きだ。
en: My older sister is outgoing and has lots of friends. My younger sister, on the other hand, likes reading alone.
why: その一方で at the start of a sentence contrasts a second, different thing: the younger sister.
そのうえ adds more about the same subject. The subject changes to 妹.
それどころか says the opposite is true about the same thing. The sisters are not opposites of one claim.
そのくせ criticises the same person for being inconsistent. The subject changes to 妹.
tell: New subject, contrasted with the last one: その一方で.

s: 売り上げが伸びている（　　）、利益はほとんど増えていない。
en: Sales are growing, but profits have barely risen.
why: 〜一方で: two things side by side, sales up and profit flat.
〜一方だ means 'more and more' and attaches to a change verb in dictionary form (増える一方だ), not to ている.
〜ついでに means 'while doing X, also do Y'. Profit is not an errand.
〜次第 attaches to a verb stem (分かり次第). It does not take ている.
tell: 一方で contrasts two facts. 一方だ means a trend that only grows.

s: この制度は利用者に歓迎されている（　　）、財源をどう確保するかという課題も残されている。
en: While users welcome the scheme, the problem of how to secure funding remains.
why: 〜一方で: the welcome side and the problem side, set against each other.
〜ことから gives a reason or source. Being welcomed is not why a funding problem exists.
〜以上 means 'since' and needs a duty or resolve after it. 残されている is neither.
〜くせに is a spoken criticism of a person. A formal report about a scheme cannot use it.
tell: A good point, then a remaining problem: 一方で.

s: 大学時代の留学（　　）、国際協力の仕事に関心を持つようになった。
en: Studying abroad at university got me interested in international aid work.
why: 〜をきっかけに: an event that set off a change. 関心を持つようになった is the change.
〜を目的に names a goal. Studying abroad is in the past and caused the interest; it was not aimed at.
〜をもとに means using something as material or a basis for making something. Interest is not made.
〜をめぐって means 'around a dispute or topic'. There is no dispute.
cue: 関心を持つようになった
tell: An event, then a change (ようになった): をきっかけに.

s: この事故（　　）、町では通学路の安全対策が見直された。
en: Prompted by this accident, the town reviewed safety on routes to school.
why: 〜を契機に is the written をきっかけに: the accident set off the review.
〜を問わず means 'regardless of'. The review happened because of the accident, not regardless of it.
〜に先立って means before an event, as preparation. Nobody reviews safety ahead of a specific accident.
〜に限らず means 'not only'. There is no second item.
tell: A trigger event, then a change: を契機に (written をきっかけに).

s: ある本との出会い（　　）、彼の人生は大きく変わった。
en: Coming across a certain book changed his life completely.
why: 〜をきっかけに: the chance meeting with a book set off the change.
〜にあたって marks a big occasion you face and prepare for (開店にあたって). A chance meeting is not planned.
〜をめぐって means 'around a dispute'. There is no dispute.
〜に沿って means following a plan or line. A life change is not following the meeting.
cue: 人生は大きく変わった
tell: Chance event, then a big change: をきっかけに. にあたって is for planned milestones.

s: 社長の交代（　　）、会社の雰囲気はがらりと変わった。
en: With the change of president, the mood at the company changed completely.
why: 〜をきっかけとして: the new president was the trigger for the change in mood.
〜を目的として names a goal. Changing presidents was not done in order to change the mood, as far as we know.
〜をはじめとして means 'starting with' one example from a list. There is no list.
〜として means 'in the role of'. The change of president is not a role.
tell: Event, then a change: をきっかけとして.

s: この施設は、地域の高齢者の健康づくり（　　）建てられた。
en: This facility was built to help older people in the area stay healthy.
why: 〜を目的として: the goal the building was built for.
〜をきっかけに needs a past event that started something. 健康づくり is a goal, not an event.
〜にこたえて needs a request or expectation (要望にこたえて). 健康づくり is not one.
〜を通じて means 'through' a medium or channel. You do not build a facility through health.
tell: A goal you build or do something for: を目的として.

s: 観光客の誘致（　　）イベントが、来月から始まる。
en: An event aimed at attracting tourists starts next month.
why: 〜を目的とした + noun: an event whose aim is attracting tourists.
〜をきっかけにした needs a past trigger. Attracting tourists is still the goal.
〜に基づいた means grounded in data or rules. Attracting tourists is not a basis.
〜に限った means limited to. The event is not limited to attracting tourists.
tell: 誘致・育成・促進 are goals: を目的とした.

s: 利益だけ（　　）経営は、長くは続かない。
en: A business run only for profit does not last long.
why: 〜を目的とする + noun: management whose only aim is profit.
〜をきっかけとする needs a trigger event. Profit is an aim, not an event.
〜にこたえる needs a request or expectation from someone. Profit is not one.
〜をめぐる means 'surrounding a dispute or issue'. The sentence is about aims, not disputes.
tell: What the business aims at: を目的とする.

s: 本講座は、初心者が基礎的な会話力を身につけること（　　）おります。
en: This course aims to help beginners gain basic conversation skills.
why: 〜を目的としております is the standard notice phrase for a course's aim.
〜をきっかけとして needs an event that set something off. Gaining skills is the aim, not a cause.
〜に先立って means before an event. Gaining skills is not an event the course comes before.
〜をめぐって means 'around a dispute'. A course description has none.
tell: Course or event descriptions: 〜ことを目的としております.

s: 外国語は、実際に使って（　　）身につくものだ。
en: You only really pick up a foreign language by actually using it.
why: 〜てこそ: only by doing X does the real result come. Using the language is what makes it stick.
〜てさえ means 'even doing X'. It points to a surprise, not to the one thing that works.
〜てまで means going as far as an extreme act. Using a language is not extreme.
〜てばかり needs いる after it (使ってばかりいる). It cannot link to 身につく.
tell: Only by actually doing it: 〜てこそ.

s: 子どもの将来を（　　）、親は厳しく叱るのだ。
en: It is precisely because they care about their children's future that parents scold them hard.
why: 〜ばこそ: the scolding happens precisely because of a good reason, caring about the future.
〜どころか says the opposite is true. Parents do care.
〜くせに criticises someone for being inconsistent. Caring and scolding are not inconsistent here.
〜ものの means 'although'. Caring and scolding do not clash; one causes the other.
tell: A harsh act explained by a good reason: 〜ばこそ.

s: 苦労があって（　　）、成功したときの喜びも大きいのだ。
en: It is precisely because there were hard times that the joy of success is so great.
why: 〜てこそ: hardship is what makes the joy big.
〜てまで means going to an extreme to get something. Hardship is not a means to joy.
〜てからでないと must be followed by a negative (できない). 大きいのだ is positive.
〜て以来 means 'ever since'. It needs a continuing state after it, not a general truth.
tell: Without X, no real Y: 〜てこそ.

s: A「どうしてそんなに選手に厳しいんですか。」B「選手を信頼して（　　）、厳しいことも言えるんですよ。」
en: A: Why are you so tough on the players? B: It is precisely because I trust them that I can say hard things.
why: 〜ばこそ: trust is the very reason the coach can be tough.
〜にもかかわらず means 'despite'. Trust is the reason, not an obstacle.
〜くせに is a criticism of someone. The coach is explaining their own reason.
〜わりに means 'considering'. There is no gap between expectation and result here.
tell: The real reason behind a tough act: 〜ばこそ.

s: A「明日までにできますか。」B「できない（　　）が、かなり急がないといけませんね。」
en: A: Can you get it done by tomorrow? B: It's not impossible, but I'd have to really hurry.
why: 〜ないことはない: a weak yes. It can be done, with effort. が then adds the catch.
〜どころではない means there is no room for something. It does not attach to できない.
〜ものか is a strong, angry 'as if!'. It does not fit a polite answer followed by が.
〜ようがない attaches to a verb stem (やりようがない). It cannot follow できない.
tell: Negative + ことはない + が: a reluctant yes.

s: この料理、食べられない（　　）が、あまり好きではない。
en: It's not that I can't eat this dish, but I'm not very fond of it.
why: 〜ないこともない: I can eat it, reluctantly. The が clause adds that I don't like it.
〜わけがない means 'no way'. 'No way I can't eat it' is too strong before あまり好きではない.
〜ものではない gives a social rule (you shouldn't). It does not fit 食べられない.
〜しかない means 'have no choice but'. It does not attach to a negative like this.
tell: Weak yes, then a reservation: 〜ないこともないが.

s: 車の運転は、できない（　　）。ただ、もう十年もしていないので自信がない。
en: It's not that I can't drive. It's just that I haven't for ten years, so I'm not confident.
why: 〜ないことはない: yes, but only just. ただ then gives the catch.
〜ないわけにはいかない means 'have to'. 'I have to not be able to drive' makes no sense.
〜に越したことはない means 'it's best to'. Being unable to drive is not best.
〜しかない does not follow a negative like できない.
tell: A grudging yes, then ただ and a reservation: 〜ないことはない.

s: A「この企画、来週までにまとめられる？」B「まとめられない（　　）けど、ほかの仕事が少し遅れるかも。」
en: A: Can you pull this proposal together by next week? B: I could, but my other work might slip a bit.
why: 〜ないこともない: a reluctant yes, with the cost added after けど.
〜はずもない means 'there's no reason to expect'. It is too strong for a hedge with けど.
〜どころじゃない means there is no room for something. It does not follow まとめられない.
〜わけがない is a flat 'no way'. A hedge followed by a cost needs a weak yes.
tell: Spoken weak yes: 〜ないこともないけど.

s: 今日の風は、涼しい（　　）寒いくらいだった。
en: Today's wind was less cool than downright cold.
why: 〜というより: 'cool' is not quite right; 'cold' fits better.
〜というと brings up a topic and what it calls to mind. It does not correct a word.
〜といっても means 'X, but less than you'd think'. Cold is more than cool, not less.
〜としても means 'even if'. Nothing here is hypothetical.
tell: Correcting your own word to a better one: 〜というより.

s: 彼は友人（　　）、兄のような存在だ。
en: He is less a friend than something like an older brother to me.
why: 〜というより: 'friend' undersells it; 'like a brother' fits better.
〜といえば brings up a related topic. It does not swap one word for a better one.
〜とすれば means 'if we suppose'. Nothing is supposed here.
〜とは defines a word. The sentence is not a definition of 友人.
tell: X is the wrong label; Y is better: 〜というより.

s: この映画は子ども向け（　　）、むしろ大人のための作品だと思う。
en: I think this film is less for children than really a work for adults.
why: 〜というより: むしろ marks the better label, adults rather than children.
〜にしては means 'for an X, surprisingly'. It cannot lead into むしろ.
〜だけあって means 'as you would expect from X'. It praises, it does not correct.
〜どころではない means there is no room for something. It does not fit a label.
tell: むしろ after the blank is the signal: 〜というより、むしろ.

s: あの店の対応は、不親切（　　）、客を客とも思っていないようだった。
en: The staff at that shop were not just unhelpful; they seemed not to see customers as customers at all.
why: 〜というより: 'unhelpful' is too mild; the next clause gives the stronger, truer label.
〜というと brings up a topic. It does not upgrade a description.
〜にしては means 'surprisingly for an X'. Nothing is surprising for a rude shop.
〜わりに means 'considering'. The second clause is not unexpected given the first.
cue: 客を客とも思っていない
tell: A mild word upgraded to a stronger one: 〜というより.

s: あんな会社で働く（　　）、アルバイトをしたほうがましだ。
en: Rather than work for a company like that, I'd sooner do part-time work.
why: 〜くらいなら: working there is so bad that part-time work is better. ほうがましだ completes it.
〜からには needs a duty or resolve after it. ほうがましだ is a preference.
〜ものなら goes with a potential verb (働けるものなら) and a wish. ほうがましだ is not a wish.
〜にしても means 'even if'. It does not set up a 'rather than'.
tell: ほうがましだ at the end: 〜くらいなら in front.

s: 途中でやめる（　　）、最初から引き受けないほうがいい。
en: Rather than quit halfway, it's better not to take it on at all.
why: 〜くらいなら: quitting halfway is so bad that not starting is better.
〜ことなく means 'without doing'. 'Without quitting, it's better not to take it on' contradicts itself.
〜ついでに means doing something extra while doing X. Quitting is not an errand.
〜うちに means 'while, before it changes'. It needs a state, not a one-off act like やめる.
tell: Bad option, then a better one with ほうがいい: 〜くらいなら.

s: 人に頭を下げて借りるくらいなら、自分で何とかする（　　）。
en: Rather than bow and borrow from someone, I'd sooner sort it out myself.
why: くらいなら needs ほうがましだ or ほうがいい to finish it: the lesser evil.
〜ものか means 'as if I would'. It would refuse the very thing the speaker prefers.
〜ことはない means 'there's no need'. It does not complete a くらいなら comparison.
〜わけがない means 'no way'. It does not complete a くらいなら comparison either.
tell: くらいなら sets up a comparison: finish with ほうがましだ.

s: A「プレゼン、緊張するなあ。」B「そんなに心配する（　　）、もう一回練習したら？」
en: A: I'm nervous about the presentation. B: Rather than worry that much, why not practise once more?
why: 〜くらいなら: instead of worrying, practising is the better option. 練習したら is the suggestion.
〜ものなら goes with a potential verb and a hope (できるものなら). 心配する is not a hope.
〜わりに means 'considering'. A suggestion cannot follow it.
〜あまり means 'so much that' and needs a result, not a suggestion like 練習したら.
tell: Instead of X, do the better thing: 〜くらいなら.

s: 疲れたときは、ゆっくりお風呂に入る（　　）。
en: When you're tired, nothing beats a long soak in the bath.
why: 〜に限る ends the sentence: the speaker says this is the best thing to do.
〜に限り means 'only, as an exception'. It cannot end the sentence.
〜に限って means 'of all times'. It needs a clause after it.
〜に限らず means 'not only'. It needs a second item after it.
tell: Sentence-final 'X is the best': に限る.

s: 夏の暑い日は、冷たいビール（　　）ね。
en: On a hot summer day, nothing beats a cold beer.
why: 〜に限ります: the speaker's view that this is the best choice for a hot day.
〜に過ぎません means 'it's only'. It belittles, the opposite of the meaning here.
〜にほかなりません means 'it is nothing other than', for stating a cause or essence. It is not a recommendation.
〜に違いありません is a confident guess. Nothing is being guessed.
tell: Situation, then the best choice for it: に限る.

s: 知らない人からのメールは、開けない（　　）。
en: With email from people you don't know, it's best not to open it.
why: 〜ないに限る: the best course is not to open it. に限る also takes the ない形.
〜ないわけにはいかない means 'must'. It would say you must open strange email.
〜どころではない means there is no room for something. It does not attach to 開けない.
〜しかない does not attach to a ない形 like 開けない.
tell: Best advice, even in the negative: 〜ないに限る.

s: やっぱり、寿司はこの店（　　）。ほかの店とは鮮度が違うよ。
en: Honestly, for sushi, nothing beats this place. The freshness is in a different league.
why: 〜に限る: this shop is the best for sushi. The next line backs it up.
〜に限らない means 'not limited to'. It clashes with ほかの店とは鮮度が違う.
〜に限っては needs a clause after it. It cannot end the sentence.
〜に限りがある means 'is limited in amount'. A shop is not an amount.
tell: Praising one choice as the best: に限る.

s: 試験まであと十日しかない。のんびり（　　）。
en: There are only ten days left until the exam. I can't afford to take it easy.
why: 〜てはいられない: the situation won't let me keep relaxing.
〜ずにはいられない means 'can't help doing'. It would say I can't help relaxing.
〜てならない is for feelings that well up (気がしてならない). のんびり is not a feeling.
〜てたまらない is for unbearable feelings (うれしくてたまらない). のんびりする is not one.
tell: Pressure ahead, so I can't keep doing X: 〜てはいられない.

s: 子どもが熱を出したと聞いて、じっとして（　　）、すぐに会社を早退した。
en: When I heard my child had a fever, I couldn't just sit still, and left work early straight away.
why: 〜てはいられず: the news made it impossible to stay still. すぐに早退した follows.
〜てばかりいて means 'doing nothing but'. It contradicts leaving at once.
〜うちに means 'while a state lasts'. It does not explain the sudden departure.
〜最中に means 'right in the middle of' an activity. Sitting still is not an activity to interrupt here.
cue: すぐに会社を早退した
tell: Can't stay put, so action follows: 〜てはいられず.

s: ライバル会社が新製品を出した。うちも黙って見て（　　）。
en: Our rival has brought out a new product. We can't just stand by and watch.
why: 〜てはいられない: the rival's move means we can't keep doing nothing.
〜てばかりだ needs いる (見てばかりいる). The form here is broken.
〜てしかたがない is for strong feelings. Watching is not a feeling.
〜てならない is for feelings that well up. Watching is not one.
cue: ライバル会社が新製品を出した
tell: A threat, so we can't keep waiting: 〜てはいられない.

s: いつまでも失敗を悔やんで（　　）。次の企画を考えよう。
en: I can't keep dwelling on my failure forever. Let's think about the next project.
why: 〜てばかりはいられない: I can't spend all my time regretting. The next line moves on.
〜てしかたがない would say I can't stop regretting. That clashes with 次の企画を考えよう.
〜てならない would say regret keeps welling up. That also clashes with moving on.
〜てたまらない would say the regret is unbearable. The speaker is moving on, not stuck.
tell: Stop doing X and move on: 〜てばかりはいられない.

s: 今年の夏は、記録的な暑さ（　　）、水不足も深刻だった。
en: This summer there was a serious water shortage on top of record heat.
why: 〜に加えて: heat, and on top of that, a water shortage. 水不足も confirms the adding.
〜に対して means 'toward' or 'in contrast to'. Heat and shortage are not opposed.
〜にとって means 'from the point of view of'. Heat has no point of view.
〜に関して means 'about, concerning'. The shortage is not about the heat.
tell: X, plus Y with も: 〜に加えて.

s: この仕事には、語学力（　　）、高いコミュニケーション能力が求められる。
en: This job requires strong communication skills in addition to language ability.
why: 〜に加え: language skill, and communication skill on top of it.
〜に反して means 'contrary to'. The two skills do not clash.
〜に限り means 'only'. It would cut out the second skill.
〜にわたり goes with a span of time or space. Language skill is not a span.
cue: 高いコミュニケーション能力が
tell: One requirement plus another: 〜に加え.

s: 本人の努力（　　）、周りの支えがあったからこそ、彼は優勝できたのだ。
en: He won because he had the support of those around him on top of his own effort.
why: 〜に加えて: effort, plus support. Both together led to the win.
〜をもとに means using something as a basis to make something. Support was not made from effort.
〜に応じて means 'in line with' something that varies. Support did not scale with effort here.
〜をめぐって means 'around a dispute'. There is no dispute.
tell: Two causes stacked: X に加えて Y.

s: 入会金（　　）、毎月三千円の会費がかかります。
en: In addition to the joining fee, there is a monthly fee of 3,000 yen.
why: 〜に加えて: a joining fee, and a monthly fee on top.
〜に限って means 'of all times', usually with a complaint. It does not fit a fee notice.
〜に際して needs an occasion such as 入会に際して. 入会金 is a fee, not an occasion.
〜を問わず means 'regardless of'. The fees are added, not ignored.
tell: Notices that add a cost: 〜に加えて.

s: 母の誕生日に、感謝の気持ち（　　）花を贈った。
en: For my mother's birthday, I sent flowers with my thanks.
why: 〜を込めて: a feeling put into a gift.
〜を通じて means 'through' a channel (知人を通じて). A feeling is not a channel.
〜をもとに means using something as material. Flowers are not made from thanks.
〜に沿って means following a plan or line. Thanks is not a plan.
tell: A feeling put into an act or a gift: 〜を込めて.

s: 祖母が心（　　）作ってくれたセーターは、今でも大切にしている。
en: I still treasure the sweater my grandmother made for me with all her heart.
why: 心を込めて is the set phrase: made with care and love.
〜を問わず means 'regardless of'. 'Regardless of heart' makes no sense.
〜にわたって needs a span of time or space. 心 is not a span.
〜に限らず means 'not only'. There is no second item.
tell: 心を込めて = with heart. A set phrase.

s: 選手たちは、被災地への励まし（　　）試合に臨んだ。
en: The players went into the match wanting to encourage the disaster-hit area.
why: 〜の思いを込めて: the players put their wish to encourage people into the match.
〜をきっかけに needs a past event that set something off. The encouragement comes from the players, after.
〜をめぐって means 'around a dispute'. There is no dispute.
〜に先立って means before an event. Encouragement is not an event the match comes before.
tell: A wish put into an act: 〜の思いを込めて.

s: この歌には、亡くなった友人への思いが（　　）。
en: This song carries the singer's feelings for a friend who died.
why: 思い is the subject, so the verb is passive: 思いが込められている.
込めている needs a person as subject and を (思いを込めている). Here the subject is 思いが.
込めさせている is causative, someone made someone put feelings in. Nothing here says that.
込まれている comes from 込む (crowded, packed in). That is a different verb.
tell: Feeling as the subject with が: 込められている (passive).

s: 彼は英語も話せ（　　）、フランス語も話せる。
en: He can speak both English and French.
why: 〜も〜ば〜も: two things of the same kind, listed. 英語も and フランス語も frame it.
〜ても means 'even if'. Being able to speak English is not an obstacle to French.
〜のに means 'although'. The two facts do not clash.
〜なら means 'if'. Nothing is hypothetical here.
tell: X も …ば Y も: both X and Y.

s: 人生には、いいとき（　　）悪いときもある。
en: In life there are good times and bad times.
why: 〜もあれば〜もある: there are both. A set pattern for two sides of life.
〜のに means 'although'. Good times are not an obstacle to bad ones.
〜さえあれば means 'as long as there is'. It sets a condition, not a list.
〜ばかりで means 'nothing but'. It clashes with 悪いときもある.
tell: 〜もあれば〜もある: there is X and there is Y.

s: あの店は、値段も（　　）、味もいいので、いつも混んでいる。
en: That restaurant is cheap and the food is good too, so it is always busy.
why: 〜も〜ければ〜も: two good points listed. 値段も and 味も frame it.
〜のに means 'although'. Cheap and tasty do not clash.
〜どころか says the opposite is true. The shop really is cheap.
〜くせに criticises. Being cheap and tasty is praise.
tell: Two も and a ば form between them: both X and Y.

s: この町には、海（　　）山もあり、一年中楽しめる。
en: This town has both the sea and the mountains, so you can enjoy it all year round.
why: 海もあれば山もある: both, and so 一年中楽しめる.
〜もなければ means 'neither'. It clashes with 山もあり.
〜はあっても is 'there may be X, but'. It needs a contrast, and 山もあり adds instead.
〜さえなく means 'not even'. It clashes with 一年中楽しめる.
tell: Two good things listed: Xもあれば Yも.
